passages.t: A new heaven and a new earth
passages.happening:
“Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and earth had passed away, and the sea was no more” (verse 1).

“I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband” (verse 2).

“And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying: ‘Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them. They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God. ‘He will wipe away every tear from their eyes,’ and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the former things have passed away’” (verses 3-4).
passages.hearers:
Everything in Revelation has been heading here, and so has everything in the Bible. The Bible's first sentence says, “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1). Its last vision is a new heaven and a new earth. The judgment of chapter 20 cleared away evil and death. Now God does what he promised through Isaiah.

The word for ‘new’, kainos, often carries the sense of new in kind or quality, renewed and fresh, rather than simply recent. Many scholars think that matters here: the new creation is the world made new, not a second world that has nothing to do with this one. The word alone cannot settle the question, and Christians read it in more than one way, as the note below sets out.

‘The sea was no more.’ In the Old Testament and in Revelation the sea is often a picture of chaos, and it was the place the beast rose from (13:1). For John, a prisoner on the island of Patmos, the sea was also what cut him off from the churches he loved. In the new creation nothing will divide God's people from one another or from him.

The holy city comes down. People do not climb up to it; God brings it down. And it comes ‘as a bride adorned for her husband’. The marriage announced in chapter 19 has come.

Then the heart of the whole vision, spoken from the throne: ‘the dwelling place of God is with man’. The word for dwelling place is the word for tent, the tabernacle where God lived among Israel in the wilderness. John's Gospel uses the related verb for the Word who became flesh and ‘made His dwelling among us’ (John 1:14). What began in the wilderness tent and came near in Jesus now fills the whole creation. ‘They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God’ is the promise God made to Israel again and again. Here it is kept in full.

And then the tears. ‘He will wipe away every tear from their eyes.’ Not tears in general. Every tear, and from their eyes, as a parent wipes a child's face. ‘No more death or mourning or crying or pain.’ This is not a promise that suffering never mattered. It is a promise that suffering was real, and that it will be ended and answered.

The Christian hope, as the creeds confess it, is not souls escaping from the world to somewhere else. It is the resurrection of the body and the life of the world to come: God coming down to live with his raised people in a creation made new.
passages.ot:
The new creation is Isaiah's promise: “For behold, I will create new heavens and a new earth. The former things will not be remembered, nor will they come to mind” (Isaiah 65:17). In the same chapter, “The sounds of weeping and crying will no longer be heard in her” (Isaiah 65:19).

The wiping of tears is Isaiah's too: “He will swallow up death forever. The Lord GOD will wipe away the tears from every face” (Isaiah 25:8). And “sorrow and sighing will flee” (Isaiah 35:10).

The bride is the prophets' picture of God's people: “as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you” (Isaiah 62:5).

And God dwelling with his people is the covenant promise of the Law and the Prophets: “I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be My people” (Leviticus 26:12), and “My dwelling place will be with them; I will be their God, and they will be My people” (Ezekiel 37:27).
passages.hard:
Will this world be renewed, or replaced? And what does this promise say to someone who is grieving?

Christians read the new creation in more than one way, and these notes do not choose. Some stress continuity: the present heaven and earth will be purified, freed from the curse and transformed, as the body that is raised is the body that was buried. They point to Paul: “the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay” (Romans 8:21), and to verse 26 below, where the glory of the nations is brought into the city. Others stress that the first heaven and earth ‘had passed away’ (verse 1), and that 2 Peter 3 speaks of the elements being destroyed by fire, so that God will make a new world after the old. Both confess a real, physical new creation and the resurrection of the body, not a heaven of souls without bodies.

If you are grieving someone who has died, these verses do not ask you to stop grieving. Jesus wept at his friend's grave (John 11:35). Paul says believers grieve, but not “like the rest, who are without hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask which tears you most long for God to wipe away, in your life or someone else's. Ask how it changes your picture of heaven to see God coming down to live with his people, rather than people escaping somewhere else. And ask what it would mean to live now as one who believes the body will be raised and the world made new.

passages.happening:
“And the One seated on the throne said, ‘Behold, I make all things new.’ Then He said, ‘Write this down, for these words are faithful and true’” (verse 5).

“And He told me, ‘It is done! I am the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End. To the thirsty I will give freely from the spring of the water of life. The one who overcomes will inherit all things, and I will be his God, and he will be My son’” (verses 6-7).

“But to the cowardly and unbelieving and abominable and murderers and sexually immoral and sorcerers and idolaters and all liars, their place will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur. This is the second death” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
This is one of the rare places in Revelation where the One seated on the throne speaks himself. And his first words are: ‘Behold, I make all things new.’ Not ‘I make new things’. All things, made new. God does not abandon the world he made.

“It is done!” The same cry came from the throne at the seventh bowl (16:17). There it meant judgment finished. Here it means the new creation begun.

‘I am the Alpha and the Omega’: the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet. God is the beginning and the end of everything. In 22:13 Jesus says the same words of himself.

Then an invitation, even here: ‘To the thirsty I will give freely from the spring of the water of life.’ Freely: without price. The gift is for the thirsty, not the deserving.

‘The one who overcomes’ takes up the promise made to each of the seven churches in chapters 2 and 3. The overcomer will ‘inherit all things’, and God says, ‘I will be his God, and he will be My son.’ The covenant promise, ‘I will be their God’, is made personal: a son and his Father.

Then verse 8, a hard list. It names those who are outside. Notice who comes first: ‘the cowardly’, the fearful. The word stands just after ‘the one who overcomes’, as its opposite. The list is a warning to the churches, spoken at the very end so that its hearers will not find themselves there.
passages.ot: The invitation to the thirsty is Isaiah's: “Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters; and you without money, come, buy, and eat!” (Isaiah 55:1). In Isaiah the invitation goes on, “Come, buy wine and milk without money and without cost!” The water of life in Revelation is given the same way.
passages.hard:
Verse 8 frightens me. I have been afraid, and I have failed. Is my place in the lake of fire?

These notes say nothing about the eternal state of any particular person. That belongs to God alone. But some things in the passage are plain. In verse 27, and again in 22:15, those outside are described as people who ‘practice’ such things. The same voice that speaks verse 8 speaks verse 6, and gives the water of life freely to anyone who is thirsty. Peter denied Jesus three times out of fear, and Jesus came to him after the resurrection and gave him his work again: “Feed My sheep” (John 21:17). And the book's invitation stays open to its last page.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask what it means to you that God's first words from the throne are ‘I make all things new’. Ask what you are thirsty for, and whether you believe the water is given freely. And ask where fear has made you a coward, and what it would mean to bring that to the one who restored Peter.

passages.happening:
One of the seven angels who had the bowls comes to John: “Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb” (verse 9). “And he carried me away in the Spirit to a mountain great and high, and showed me the holy city of Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God, shining with the glory of God. Its radiance was like a most precious jewel, like a jasper, as clear as crystal” (verses 10-11).

“The city had a great and high wall with twelve gates inscribed with the names of the twelve tribes of Israel, and twelve angels at the gates” (verse 12). There are three gates on each side: east, north, south and west (verse 13). “The wall of the city had twelve foundations bearing the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The angel uses almost exactly the words of 17:1, where another bowl angel said, ‘Come, I will show you’ the great prostitute. The two scenes are meant to be read side by side. Babylon was seen in a wilderness; the bride is seen from ‘a mountain great and high’. Babylon was dressed in borrowed luxury and drunk on the blood of the saints. The bride shines ‘with the glory of God’.

And notice: the angel says ‘the bride’, and John is shown a city. The new Jerusalem is not mainly a place. It is a people joined to God. The city is the bride.

Its radiance is ‘like a jasper, as clear as crystal’. In 4:3 the one on the throne looked like jasper. The city shines with God's own light.

The gates bear the names of the twelve tribes of Israel. The foundations bear the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb. Israel and the church, old covenant and new, form one city. No one is left out of the story God has been telling from Abraham on. There are three gates on every side: east, north, south and west. The city is open toward the whole world.
passages.ot:
The gates named for the tribes come from Ezekiel's closing vision of the city: “the gates of the city will be named after the tribes of Israel” (Ezekiel 48:31).

And the jewelled city is Isaiah's promise to the afflicted city: “surely I will set your stones in antimony and lay your foundations with sapphires. I will make your pinnacles of rubies, your gates of sparkling jewels, and all your walls of precious stones” (Isaiah 54:11-12).
passages.asks: Ask what it means to you that the city is a bride, a people rather than a place. Ask how the names of Israel's tribes and the Lamb's apostles on the same walls shape how you see the people of God. And ask which of the two cities, the bride or Babylon, your life is being built toward.

passages.happening:
“The angel who spoke with me had a golden measuring rod to measure the city and its gates and walls” (verse 15).

“The city lies foursquare, with its width the same as its length. And he measured the city with the rod, and all its dimensions were equal—12,000 stadia in length and width and height” (verse 16). “And he measured its wall to be 144 cubits, by the human measure the angel was using” (verse 17).

“The wall was made of jasper, and the city itself of pure gold, as pure as glass” (verse 18). The twelve foundations are adorned with twelve precious stones, from jasper and sapphire to topaz and amethyst (verses 19-20). “And the twelve gates were twelve pearls, with each gate consisting of a single pearl. The main street of the city was pure gold, as clear as glass” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
In chapter 11 John measured the temple, as a sign that God's people were known and kept. Now an angel measures the whole city with a golden rod.

The city is a cube: its length, width and height are the same. The inner sanctuary of Solomon's temple, the Most Holy Place where God's presence dwelt, was a cube too. So the whole city has become the Most Holy Place. Once only the high priest entered it, once a year. Now God's people live there.

The measures are given in the units of John's day. A stadion was about 185 metres, so 12,000 stadia is roughly 2,200 kilometres, or about 1,400 miles: a city far larger than any on earth. The wall is 144 cubits, about 65 metres, though the text does not say whether that is its height or thickness. And look at the numbers: twelve thousand, and twelve times twelve. In Revelation twelve belongs to the people of God.

The twelve foundation stones recall the twelve gems on the high priest's breastpiece, each engraved with the name of a tribe. The ancient names of precious stones do not always match modern ones, so exact identifications are uncertain. The gates are each a single pearl. The street is gold, ‘as clear as glass’. Gold that is clear like glass is not something anyone has seen. The description keeps reaching past what words can hold.
passages.ot:
The cube is the shape of the Most Holy Place: “The inner sanctuary was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high. He overlaid the inside with pure gold” (1 Kings 6:20).

And the stones of the breastpiece bore the tribes' names: “The twelve stones are to correspond to the names of the sons of Israel, each engraved like a seal with the name of one of the twelve tribes” (Exodus 28:21).
passages.hard:
Is the new Jerusalem a real city of these measurements?

Readers take the city in different ways, and these notes do not choose. Some expect a real city of the size given, the capital of the new earth. Many others note that the measurements, materials and numbers are all symbolic, a cube like the Most Holy Place, twelves for the people of God, a street of gold as clear as glass, and read the city as a picture of the people of God made perfect and filled with his presence, since the city is also the bride. Many hold something of both: a real new creation, described in pictures that say more than a map could.

Most interpreters across the traditions agree on the central point. The Christian hope is bodily, earthly in a renewed sense, and shared with others. It is not an escape of souls from the world God made.
passages.asks: Ask what it means to you that the whole city is the Most Holy Place, open to all God's people. Ask whether you picture the life to come as smaller and thinner than this life, or larger and more solid. And ask how the hope of this city might change the way you treat the place and people where you live now.

passages.happening:
“But I saw no temple in the city, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple” (verse 22).

“And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, because the glory of God illuminates the city, and the Lamb is its lamp” (verse 23).

“By its light the nations will walk, and into it the kings of the earth will bring their glory. Its gates will never be shut at the end of the day, because there will be no night there. And into the city will be brought the glory and honor of the nations” (verses 24-26).

“But nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who practices an abomination or a lie, but only those whose names are written in the Lamb’s Book of Life” (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
For anyone who knew Jerusalem, this is the most startling line in the vision: ‘I saw no temple in the city.’ The Greek word, naos, means the inner shrine where a god was thought to live. There is no temple because there is no need for one. ‘The Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple.’ God's presence fills everything. There is no longer any separate holy place, because the whole city is holy.

The city needs no sun or moon. ‘The glory of God illuminates the city, and the Lamb is its lamp.’ In Babylon the light of a lamp went out for ever (18:23). Here the Lamb himself is the lamp.

Then a surprise. ‘The kings of the earth will bring their glory’ into the city. In this book the kings of the earth have been Babylon's lovers and the beast's allies. Yet here they bring their glory into the city of God, and ‘the glory and honor of the nations’ is brought in. Many readers see in this the hope that what was good in human life and culture will be cleansed and offered to God, not thrown away.

The gates are never shut, because there is no night. This city has no enemies left to keep out, and no darkness to fear.

And yet ‘nothing unclean will ever enter it’. The open gates are not careless. Those who enter are ‘those whose names are written in the Lamb’s Book of Life’. The book belongs to the Lamb. Entry is his gift.
passages.ot:
The light of the city is Isaiah's vision: “No longer will the sun be your light by day, nor the brightness of the moon shine on your night; for the LORD will be your everlasting light, and your God will be your splendor” (Isaiah 60:19).

So are the open gates and the nations' gifts: “Your gates will always stand open; they will never be shut, day or night, so that the wealth of the nations may be brought into you, with their kings being led in procession” (Isaiah 60:11). “Nations will come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your dawn” (Isaiah 60:3).

And the city kept clean is Isaiah's promise to Zion: “For the uncircumcised and unclean will no longer enter you” (Isaiah 52:1).
passages.asks: Ask what it would mean to live with God so near that no temple is needed. Ask what good things in your own work and culture you hope will be brought into the city, cleansed. And ask whether you know your name is written in the Lamb's book, and what it would mean to trust that it is his gift.
